The commonest mistake is not the one people expect. It is not the strength on the bottle. It is that people put sunscreen on once, in the morning, at home, and treat the day as done. It wears off. About two hours, and far faster than that if you swim or if you sweat, and after that you are walking around with the feeling of being protected and none of the protection. So it goes on again, during the day. Put the bottle where you will trip over it. The second thing, and I say this every time and it never lands the first time, is that a tan is not protection. A tan is damage you can see. That is the whole sentence. Your skin went darker because the cells underneath were injured and the body responded. There is no such thing as a safe tan, and a base tan before a holiday protects you from almost nothing. And the third thing is what to do about a mole, because people wait to be certain, and certainty is not the job. Photograph it. Monitor it over three months. If it changes shape, colour or size, come in. Do not wait until you are sure. By the time you are sure, you have spent six months being sure.

Everybody's first instinct is to lead with the frightening thing, and it does not work. It is not that people are irrational. It is that fear without an action produces avoidance: you look away, you close the tab, you change the channel, and you feel slightly worse and do nothing at all. We have measured this over and over. A campaign that only frightens people moves nothing. Every message that works has exactly two halves, and if either one is missing the whole thing collapses. One: a consequence that is real and specific enough to picture. Not cancer kills. If you spend the afternoon out there today, you will burn, and that burn counts for the rest of your life. Two: one action small enough to do today. Not change your relationship with the sun. Put the bottle by the door. And there is one word I would put in every leaflet if they let me, which is preventable. Preventable is the most useful word in this field, because it tells the person reading that the ending has not been written yet. It is the difference between a warning and a sentence.
